# Three structures, three questions

Section 43 had one object, the prefix function, and everything came out of it.
This section is the opposite: three unrelated structures, and the skill being
taught is choosing between them. Picking the wrong one is not a slow solution,
it is usually an impossible one.

The question to ask first is never "which structure do I know?" but **what
object is the query about?**


```{=latex}

     separate words --- it is built from one string. A trie cannot compare two
     arbitrary substrings of one long text --- it indexes prefixes, not
     positions. Before writing code, say out loud which object the query names:
     a prefix of a dictionary word, a window inside one text, or the set of all

\end{tikzpicture}

```

| The query names | Reach for | Section problem |
|---|---|---|
| a prefix of a dictionary word | trie | A, D |
| a window inside one text | rolling hash, or direct comparison | B |
| the set of all substrings of one text | suffix automaton or suffix array | C |

Each of the three chapters below takes one row of that table.

# Tries: prefixes of many words

A trie is a rooted tree whose edges carry single characters, so a node *is* the
prefix spelled along the path from the root to it. Shared prefixes are stored
once, which is the entire point.

To answer "how many dictionary words begin with `p`", store on each node the
number of inserted words whose path passes through it:

```text
insert(word):
    node = root
    for c in word:
        create edge c if missing
        node = child[node][c]
        cnt[node] += 1

query(p):
    node = root
    for c in p:
        if edge c missing: return 0
        node = child[node][c]
    return cnt[node]
```


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  nd/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=6.6mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  walk/.style={nd,fill=orange!30,very thick},
  ew/.style={nd,double,double distance=1pt},
  ed/.style={draw,gray!60},
  edH/.style={draw,very thick,orange!80!black},
  ct/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=blue!55!black},
  dep/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!55,anchor=east}]

  \node[nd]   (r)   at (2.05, 0)    {};
  \node[walk] (a1)  at (0.7,-1.1)   {\texttt{a}};
  \node[nd]   (b1)  at (3.4,-1.1)   {\texttt{b}};
  \node[walk] (p1)  at (0.7,-2.2)   {\texttt{p}};
  \node[nd]   (a2)  at (3.4,-2.2)   {\texttt{a}};
  \node[ew]   (p2)  at (0,  -3.3)   {\texttt{p}};
  \node[ew]   (e1)  at (1.4,-3.3)   {\texttt{e}};
  \node[ew]   (t1)  at (3.4,-3.3)   {\texttt{t}};
  \node[nd]   (l1)  at (0,  -4.4)   {\texttt{l}};
  \node[ew]   (e2)  at (0,  -5.5)   {\texttt{e}};

  \draw[edH] (r) -- (a1);  \draw[edH] (a1) -- (p1);
  \foreach \x/\y in {r/b1,p1/p2,p1/e1,b1/a2,a2/t1,p2/l1,l1/e2} \draw[ed] (\x) -- (\y);

  \node[ct] at (0.28,-0.95) {$3$};
  \node[ct] at (3.82,-1.1)  {$1$};
  \node[ct] at (0.28,-2.2)  {$3$};
  \node[ct] at (3.82,-2.2)  {$1$};
  \node[ct] at (-.42,-3.3)  {$2$};
  \node[ct] at (1.82,-3.3)  {$1$};
  \node[ct] at (3.82,-3.3)  {$1$};
  \node[ct] at (-.42,-4.4)  {$1$};
  \node[ct] at (-.42,-5.5)  {$1$};
  \node[font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60,anchor=west] at (2.45,0) {root (empty prefix)};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=7.4cm] at (4.6,-0.55)
    {\textbf{Dictionary:} \texttt{app}, \texttt{apple}, \texttt{ape},
     \texttt{bat}.\\[3pt]
     Each edge carries one character, so a node \emph{is} the prefix spelled on
     the path down to it. The \textcolor{blue!55!black}{blue number} is
     \texttt{cnt[v]}: how many inserted words pass through \texttt{v}.\\[4pt]
     \textbf{Query = walk.} \texttt{"ap"} follows the
     \textcolor{orange!65!black}{thick path} and reports
     $\texttt{cnt}=3$ (\texttt{app}, \texttt{apple}, \texttt{ape}).
     \texttt{"app"} reports $2$; \texttt{"b"} reports $1$.
     \texttt{"z"} has no edge out of the root, so the answer is $0$ without
     any further work.\\[4pt]
     \textbf{Not an end-of-word counter.} Double circles mark where a word
     ends. \texttt{cnt} at \texttt{app} is $2$, not $1$, because
     \texttt{apple} passes through on its way down.\\[4pt]
     The root is left at $0$: an empty-prefix query is $n$ by definition and
     never needs the trie.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Two details decide whether this is correct.

**`cnt` is not an end-of-word counter.** It counts words *passing through*, so a
node can hold a count larger than the number of words ending there. In the
figure, `app` has `cnt = 2` because `apple` continues below it. If you need to
know how many words *end* at a node, that is a second, separate counter.

**The root is never incremented.** The loop moves to a child before
incrementing, so `cnt[root]` stays `0`. The empty prefix is shared by all `n`
words and no query needs the trie to discover it. A missing edge ends a query
immediately with `0`, with no need to walk the rest of the pattern.

# Palindrome queries

For a substring `s[l..r]`, the direct test walks two pointers inward and stops
at the first disagreement:


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,x=1cm,y=1cm,
  c/.style={draw,minimum width=.8cm,minimum height=.6cm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  sel/.style={c,fill=green!28},
  bad/.style={c,fill=red!22},
  pl/.style={c,fill=white},
  gh/.style={c,draw=gray!30,text=gray!40},
  hd/.style={draw=none,minimum width=.8cm,inner sep=0pt,font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60},
  rl/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!65,anchor=east},
  arc/.style={draw,thick,gray!70},
  ok/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=green!30!black},
  no/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=red!60!black}]

  \foreach \i in {1,...,7} \node[hd] at (.8*\i-.8,.62) {$\i$};
  \foreach \i in {0,...,6} \node[hd,text=gray!40] at (.8*\i,-.52) {$\i$};
  \foreach \ch/\i in {a/0,b/1,a/2,c/3,a/4,b/5,a/6} \node[pl] at (.8*\i,0) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[rl] at (-.5,.62) {1-based};
  \node[rl] at (-.5,0)   {$s$};
  \node[rl] at (-.5,-.52){0-based};

  % query [3,5]
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/gh,b/1/gh,a/2/sel,c/3/sel,a/4/sel,b/5/gh,a/6/gh}
    \node[\st] at (.8*\i,-1.65) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[rl] at (-.5,-1.65) {query $[3,5]$};
  \draw[arc] (1.6,-1.99) to[bend right=42] node[below=1pt,ok] {$\texttt{a}=\texttt{a}$} (3.2,-1.99);
  \node[ok,anchor=west] at (5.05,-1.65) {pointers meet $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{YES}};

  % query [2,4]
  \foreach \ch/\i/\st in {a/0/gh,b/1/bad,a/2/bad,c/3/bad,a/4/gh,b/5/gh,a/6/gh}
    \node[\st] at (.8*\i,-3.15) {\texttt{\ch}};
  \node[rl] at (-.5,-3.15) {query $[2,4]$};
  \draw[arc] (0.8,-3.49) to[bend right=42] node[below=1pt,no] {$\texttt{b}\neq\texttt{c}$} (2.4,-3.49);
  \node[no,anchor=west] at (5.05,-3.15) {first pair fails $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{NO}};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt,text width=12.4cm] at (-1.55,-4.2)
    {\textbf{Convert the indices first.} Statements here give $[l,r]$ 1-based and
     inclusive; arrays are 0-based. Subtract one from each end \emph{before}
     comparing, and compare $s[l]$ with $s[r]$, then move inward while
     $l<r$. A single off-by-one turns every odd-length answer wrong while
     leaving even-length ones correct, which is why both parities must be
     tested.\\[3pt]
     \textbf{Direct or hashed.} The direct scan is $O(r-l+1)$ per query and
     exact, which is why the local bounds allow it. For large query loads
     compare a forward hash of $[l,r]$ against a reverse hash of the mirrored
     range $[n-1-r,\,n-1-l]$ --- fast, but probabilistic; Manacher or a
     palindromic tree is the deterministic alternative.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

```text
while l < r:
    if s[l] != s[r]: return NO
    l += 1
    r -= 1
return YES
```

This is `O(r-l+1)` per query and exactly right, which is why the local bounds
allow it. It is also completely transparent: the equality condition is visible
rather than hidden behind a hash.

When the query load is too large for that, compare a forward hash of `[l,r]`
against a reverse hash of the mirrored range:

```text
hash_forward(l, r) == hash_reverse(n-1-r, n-1-l)
```

Hashing is `O(1)` per query after `O(n)` preprocessing, but it is
probabilistic. Manacher's algorithm and palindromic trees are the deterministic
alternatives. When the constraints permit the direct check, prefer it.

# Suffix automata: all substrings of one string

A suffix automaton is a compressed automaton that accepts exactly the
substrings of one string, in `O(n)` states. Two arrays describe it:

- `len[v]`, the length of the longest substring represented by state `v`;
- `link[v]`, the state representing the longest proper suffix that lives in a
  different state.

The states partition every substring, and the count of distinct non-empty
substrings falls straight out:

```text
answer = sum over v != root of ( len[v] - len[link[v]] )
```


```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small,
  st/.style={circle,draw,fill=white,minimum size=8mm,inner sep=0pt,font=\small},
  root/.style={st,fill=gray!18},
  tr/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,thick},
  sl/.style={draw,->,>=Latex,densely dashed,blue!60},
  tl/.style={font=\scriptsize,fill=white,inner sep=1.2pt},
  ll/.style={font=\scriptsize,text=gray!60}]

  \node[root] (s0) at (0,0)      {$0$};
  \node[st]   (s1) at (2.3,1.15) {$1$};
  \node[st]   (s2) at (2.3,-1.15){$2$};
  \node[st]   (s3) at (4.6,0)    {$3$};

  \draw[tr] (s0) -- node[tl] {\texttt{a}} (s1);
  \draw[tr] (s0) -- node[tl] {\texttt{b}} (s2);
  \draw[tr] (s1) -- node[tl] {\texttt{b}} (s2);
  \draw[tr] (s2) -- node[tl] {\texttt{a}} (s3);

  \draw[sl] (s1) to[bend right=38] (s0);
  \draw[sl] (s2) to[bend left=38]  (s0);
  \draw[sl] (s3) to[bend right=38] (s1);

  \node[ll] at (2.3,1.72) {$\mathtt{len}=1$};
  \node[ll] at (2.3,-1.72){$\mathtt{len}=2$};
  \node[ll] at (4.6,-0.62) {$\mathtt{len}=3$};
  \node[ll] at (0,0.62)   {$\mathtt{len}=0$};

  \node[font=\scriptsize,anchor=north west,align=left] at (-0.9,-2.15)
    {\tikz\draw[tr] (0,0) -- (.5,0);\ transition (read a character)\qquad
     \tikz\draw[sl] (0,0) -- (.5,0);\ suffix link};

  \node[draw=gray!45,rounded corners,fill=gray!4,align=left,font=\scriptsize,
        anchor=north west,inner sep=5pt] at (6.1,1.65)
    {\textbf{Suffix automaton of \texttt{aba}}\\[3pt]
     \begin{tabular}{@{}ccccl@{}}
       $v$ & $\mathtt{len}$ & $\mathtt{link}$ & $\mathtt{len}[v]-\mathtt{len}[\mathtt{link}]$ & represents\\[1pt]
       $1$ & $1$ & $0$ & $1$ & \texttt{a}\\
       $2$ & $2$ & $0$ & $2$ & \texttt{b},\ \texttt{ab}\\
       $3$ & $3$ & $1$ & $2$ & \texttt{ba},\ \texttt{aba}\\[2pt]
       \multicolumn{3}{@{}r}{total} & $\mathbf{5}$ & \\
     \end{tabular}\\[4pt]
     Enumerating by hand gives the same five:\\
     \texttt{a},\ \texttt{b},\ \texttt{ab},\ \texttt{ba},\ \texttt{aba}.\\[4pt]
     One state holds a whole run of lengths that\\
     end at the same set of positions, and
     $\mathtt{link}$\\
     points at the next shorter run. So the state\\
     adds exactly the lengths its link does not\\
     already cover --- no substring is counted twice.\\[3pt]
     State $0$ is excluded: it is the empty string.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The reason this does not double count is worth stating plainly: a single state
holds a whole *run* of lengths whose occurrences end at the same set of
positions, and `link[v]` points at the state holding the next shorter run. So
state `v` contributes exactly the lengths its link does not already cover. The
root is excluded because it represents the empty string.

Check the formula against a string small enough to enumerate. `ababa` has
distinct substrings `a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab, abab, baba, ababa`, nine of them,
and the automaton's contributions sum to nine. `aaa` gives `a, aa, aaa`, three.

**Cloning.** When an existing transition would break the invariant
`len[p] + 1 == len[q]`, construction splits `q` into a clone carrying the same
transitions but a shorter `len`, then redirects the affected suffix links. This
is not an implementation trick; it is what keeps one state from representing two
different sets of end positions. `abb` is the shortest string that forces one.

At the bounds used locally, problem C can also be solved by a set of substrings
or a suffix array. The formula above is still the thing to know, because it is
what scales.

# Implementation notes and tests

**Tries in C++.** For lowercase input, `vector<array<int,26>>` with node `0` as
the root and `0` meaning "absent" is compact and fast. Reserve capacity for the
total input length; that is the exact upper bound on node count.

**Tries in Python.** A `dict` per node is clearer and usually faster than a
26-slot list for sparse alphabets. Build children with `setdefault`.

**Everything else.** Read input with `sys.stdin.buffer.read()`. For hashing, use
two independent moduli or a random base — a single fixed 32-bit modulus is
attackable. Palindrome endpoints arrive 1-based and inclusive; convert once, at
the point of reading, not repeatedly inside the loop.

| Case | What it catches |
|---|---|
| a word that is a prefix of another word (`app`, `apple`) | treating `cnt` as an end-of-word counter |
| duplicate words in the dictionary | a unique-prefix answer that must be `-1` |
| query prefix absent from the trie | a missing-edge path that walks past the end |
| single-character palindrome query | the `l < r` loop bound |
| even-length palindrome (`abba`) | an off-by-one that only breaks one parity |
| odd-length palindrome (`aba`) | the same off-by-one, the other parity |
| all-equal string (`aaaa`) | the maximal-state-sharing case |
| one-character string | an empty contribution sum |

Useful values to check by hand: the trie over `app, apple, ape, bat` gives
`cnt["ap"] = 3` and `cnt["app"] = 2`; `abacaba` answers NO for `[2,4]` and YES
for `[3,5]`; and `aba` has exactly `5` distinct non-empty substrings.

Run the local reference suite with:

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/44_string_algorithms_ii/check.py
```

# Exercises

Use A to fix the trie invariant before writing anything: `cnt[v]` counts words
passing through `v`, not words ending at `v`. Use B to convert the 1-based
inclusive endpoints exactly once and to test both parities. Use C to state the
`len[v] - len[link[v]]` invariant even if you solve it with a set at these
bounds, because that sentence is what transfers to large inputs. Use D as the
blind synthesis problem: the shortest unique prefix of a word is the first node
on its path whose count has fallen to one, so decide what the trie must store
and what it means when the count never falls. Test a word that is a prefix of
another, duplicate words, a prefix that is absent, and single-character inputs.

- A. Trie Prefix Count: Given dictionary words and prefix queries, count words having each prefix.
- B. Palindrome Queries: For each substring query, print whether the substring is a palindrome.
- C. Distinct Substrings: Print the number of distinct non-empty substrings of a string.
- D. Unique Prefix Lengths: For each word, print the length of its shortest prefix shared by exactly one input word, or `-1`.
